root.note: Further back the Latin word has no secure etymology.

history: In Latin, casa was a humble word: a hut, a shepherd's cottage. A proper Roman house was a domus. The people of the countryside kept talking about their casa, and when Latin turned into Portuguese, the small word won. Today a casa is any house or flat, and also home: estou em casa, ‘I'm at home’, vou para casa, ‘I'm going home’. Spanish and Italian kept casa too. French went its own way: its house is maison, but the old casa hides in chez, ‘at the home of’. Domus did not disappear either. It lives on in doméstico, ‘domestic’, and in a weekday: domingo, the Lord's day, comes from the same family.
historyEinfach: Casa means ‘house’ or ‘home’. The word comes from Latin. In Latin, casa was a small, simple house, a hut. A big Roman house had another name: domus. Later, casa became the normal word. In Portuguese you say estou em casa, ‘I am at home’. Spanish and Italian also say casa.

elsewhere.text: French chez moi, ‘at my place’, is the Latin casa worn down to one syllable.
The grand Roman word for a house lost to casa, but it survives in other Portuguese words.
